note: ça marche and OK are just as everyday.
note the apostrophe; it's one word.
and quelque chose = something.
spoken French's all-purpose noun: c'est quoi ce truc ? j'ai un truc à faire. Learn it early – you'll hear it constantly.
feminine: de l'eau fraîche. In a café ask for une carafe d'eau – tap water, free.
masculine. la monnaie = change (coins).
un bel endroit. Careful: une place is a seat or a square, not 'a place' in general.
the polite refusal; a bare non sounds blunt.
the same two words answer the question. ça va bien for a bit more warmth.
past: qu'est-ce qui s'est passé ? For 'what's wrong?' say qu'est-ce qu'il y a ?
how it's really said. qu'est-ce que c'est ? is the tidy written order.
tu t'appelles comment ? with tu. The doubled vous vous is correct, not a typo.
French 'has' its states rather than 'being' them: j'ai faim, j'ai soif, j'ai froid, j'ai peur.
the standard line for leaving. bon, je dois y aller softens it.
parce qu'il pleut. Never starts an answer with 'car' in speech.
mon père when talking about him to others.
the obligatory French table ritual, said before anyone starts eating, even to strangers at the next café table. French has no 'have you eaten?' greeting; this is the food ritual you actually need.
no article after parler: parle français, not 'parle le français'.
or just plus lentement, s'il vous plaît. The single most useful sentence in week one.
the full form is je n'ai pas compris; spoken French drops the ne almost every time.

word: ça se dit comment en français ?
roman: ca se dit comment en francais ?
en: how do you say this in French?
note: or comment on dit ... en français ? Both are everyday.
copain/copine is the everyday word; un ami is a shade more serious. Watch out: mon copain also means boyfriend.
the ç keeps the s sound; don't use it to call a waiter, that's long dead.
also 'daughter'.
le téléphone on its own suggests the landline. le portable also means a laptop – context decides.
phone only. Saying allô to someone's face is a giveaway that you learned French from a textbook.
le p'tit-déj in speech. le déjeuner is lunch and le dîner is dinner – don't be caught out by the overlap.
c'est très bon is said far more often and lands just as well.
avoir again, not être.
dix euros; the s is silent. Prices are often said as 'dix euros cinquante'.
c'est combien ? is shorter and just as common.
vous parlez anglais ? – no article after parler.

word: je suis / tu es / il est / on est / vous êtes / ils sont
roman: je suis / tu es / il est / on est / vous etes / ils sont
en: present of être: am, are, is
note: on est, not 'on sont' – on always takes the il/elle form even though it means 'we'.
often crushed to 'chais pas'. aucune idée = no idea.
here the article stays, because the verb isn't parler: j'apprends le français.
rising intonation is all you need – no est-ce que required.
je suis anglais / anglaise also works. Say britannique if you'd rather not say England.
the spoken shape. où sont les toilettes ? is the tidy one.
un instant is slightly more formal; ne quittez pas on the phone.
au secours ! is the shout in a real emergency.
the French offer is coffee, not tea. tu prends quelque chose ? covers any drink.
the standard order; c'est quoi ? is the everyday spoken one.
spoken order. quelle heure est-il ? is the formal inversion.
what you call her to her face, and within the family.
j'ai, t'as, il a, on a. t'as is how tu as is really pronounced: t'as l'heure ?
full form il n'y a pas; spoken French drops the ne, and often the whole thing lands as 'y a pas'. c'est pas = it isn't.
point and say celui-là for a masculine thing, celle-là for a feminine one. Essential at a market stall.

en: past tense: avoir + participle, but être with go/come-type verbs, and then it agrees
note: re-tiered up – you need the past within the first fortnight, and it's the only past used in speech. être verbs: aller, venir, partir, arriver, rester, entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, tomber, naître, mourir, plus every reflexive (je me suis levé).

en: future: je vais manger, on va y aller
note: aller + verb is what people actually say for anything ahead. The one-word future (je mangerai) is more distant or formal – learn it later.

word: j'ai faim / j'ai froid / j'ai mal
roman: j'ai faim / j'ai froid / j'ai mal
en: 'I have' frame for states: hungry, cold, in pain
note: French uses avoir where English uses 'be': j'ai chaud, j'ai soif, j'ai sommeil, j'ai de la fièvre

word: le pain → les pains / la bière → les bières
roman: le pain / la bière → les pains
en: noun gender and plural: le/la, plural -s (silent)
note: gender is unpredictable, so learn le/la with the word; the plural -s isn't pronounced – les does the work
the daily bread run: une baguette, s'il vous plaît. Ask for pas trop cuite / bien cuite

en: greet with a kiss on each cheek
note: the French respect-and-affection ritual: two kisses in most regions, three or four in some; men often shake hands instead. Follow their lead
The daily staple bread; 'une tradition' is the better, slower-made one. Bought fresh, often twice a day

en: to greet with a kiss on each cheek
note: The family and friends greeting. Two kisses in most regions, three or four in some; men often shake hands with each other instead. Follow whoever leans in, and do it on arriving and on leaving.

word: pour aller à la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
roman: pour aller à la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
en: how do I get to the station, please?
note: The standard way to ask directions, and it needs no verb at all: pour aller à + place. Swap in la poste, la plage, le centre-ville. Currently hidden in a note under pour.
The syllabus teaches only the past (j'ai pas compris). This is the one you need in the moment: je comprends pas, désolé. Written je ne comprends pas.
French politeness rides on adding madame/monsieur rather than a particle: oui monsieur, merci madame.
the everyday hesitation opener: ben oui, ben non, ben je sais pas. To call out to someone it's eh ! or oh !
describes birth order only – French has no didi-style term for addressing an older woman. To address one you use madame or her first name.
same as grande sœur: a description, never a form of address.
replaces dal as the weekday staple: this is what actually turns up on a French family table. les lentilles exist but are occasional.
vous en voulez encore ? with vous. The little en means 'of it' and cannot be dropped.
mes affaires = my things. les bagages / les valises for luggage.
sers-toi with tu. The host's line at a French table.
on the phone; in the family you'd just say c'est Tom.
les frites = chips, la purée = mash.
the dish adjustment you actually need in France, in place of 'not too spicy': saignant (rare), à point (medium), bien cuit (well done).
feminine. au secours ! is the shout; à l'aide ! is more literary.

en: respect goes on the title plus the surname
note: the nearest thing to ji: monsieur/madame attaches to the surname, never the first name. And a bare bonjour sounds curt – bonjour madame is the polite minimum.
only ever appears in avoir faim; never 'je suis faim'.
tacked on the end for agreement or softening: c'est bon, hein ? Also a blunt 'what?' if you didn't hear.

en: to be in the middle of doing: je suis en train de manger
note: French usually needs nothing at all – je mange covers both 'I eat' and 'I'm eating'. Use en train de only when the ongoing-ness is the point.

word: j'étais / tu étais / il était / on était / vous étiez / ils étaient
roman: j'etais / tu etais / il etait / on etait / vous etiez / ils etaient
note: c'était is the single most useful past form in the language: c'était bien, c'était bon, c'était comment ?
il a l'air fatigué = he looks tired. ça m'a l'air bien = that looks good to me.
reflexive – you seat yourself: je m'assieds, assieds-toi, asseyez-vous.
casual, between friends. ça roule ? is very familiar indeed.
bien actually weakens it: j'aime bien = I like, j'aime = I love. Counter-intuitive but consistent.
prenez soin de vous with vous. Warm rather than routine – bonne journée is the everyday sign-off.
jusqu'à demain, jusqu'à la gare. Contracts with le: jusqu'au marché.
on + question intonation does the job of the Hindi subjunctive: on mange ? on se voit demain ? For permission, je peux ? The real subjonctif (il faut que je fasse) comes much later.
je dois y aller is the firmer 'I have to go' and the usual line for leaving a gathering.
note the partitive de l'. In a restaurant, une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît gets you free tap water.
à tout à l'heure = see you later today; à plus tard is the goodbye version.
avant de partir, before a verb; plain avant before a noun: avant le dîner.
des fois is the spoken one; parfois is neutral, quelquefois a bit tidier.
dans cinq minutes.
une demi-heure; on the clock it follows: trois heures et demie. un demi in a bar is a small beer.
also means stepmother – French doesn't distinguish. Same pattern for beau-frère, belle-sœur.
and stepfather, likewise.
un sucre = a sugar lump, which is what arrives with a coffee.
sucré for taste; the opposite in a food context is salé (savoury), not amer.

en: that was lovely, thank you – I've had plenty
note: the way to decline more at a French table. Never say je suis plein – it means you're drunk, and of a woman, pregnant. non merci, ça va works too.
juste un peu = just a little, when you're being offered more.
une boutique is small and smart; the supermarket is un supermarché.
exactement and tout à fait are the other everyday agreements.
je me suis bien amusé(e) is the fuller version; c'était super is what people say.
ça vous a plu ? with vous. c'était comment ? = how was it?
always plural. bravo ! for an achievement in the moment.
ça va mieux ? = are you feeling better? vous vous sentez comment ? with vous.
la pharmacie, with its green cross, is where you buy them and where you can ask advice.
en été. la chaleur = heat, il fait chaud = it's hot.
en hiver. The full set is le printemps (au printemps, the odd one out), l'été, l'automne, l'hiver.
prendre une photo; je peux prendre une photo ?
du coup is the ubiquitous spoken version and you'll hear it constantly.
what you turn up with at a French home, the way mithai works in India – that, or flowers, or a good bottle. Never arrive empty-handed.
spoken form – written/formal is je ne me sens pas bien

en: how much does that come to?
note: what you ask at the till for a total
spoken order; quelle heure est-il ? is the textbook version
to a taxi driver; add s'il vous plaît
c'est un peu plus loin

en: what do you do for a living?
note: tu fais quoi comme travail ? with family and friends
question word goes on the end in speech
à + city, en + feminine country: j'habite en Angleterre
weather always uses il fait: il fait beau, il fait froid

word: le train est à quelle heure ?
roman: le train est à quelle heure ?

word: un kilo de tomates, s'il vous plaît
roman: un kilo de tomates, s'il vous plaît
note: the market frame: quantity + de + food, no article after de
pronounced 'o-nyon' – the g is silent
la carte bleue / la CB; sans contact = contactless
cuisiner is the neutral verb; je fais à manger ce soir
arrête ! = stop it!
swap the noun: mon passeport, mes clés, mon téléphone
plural des œufs – the f goes silent
encore un peu = a bit more
declining a second helping; c'était très bon, merci softens it

word: vous pouvez m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?
roman: vous pouvez m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?

note: un tout petit peu = a tiny bit
heures is plural from two on

en: elder/younger marked by grand/petit before the kin term
note: only siblings work this way; cousins and everyone else take no age marking, unlike Hindi
French marks no maternal/paternal side; say mon grand-père paternel or just use his name
French splits grandparent words by formality, not by side: grand-père to talk about him, papi to his face
often papi/mamie + first name: mamie Jeanne

en: excuse me! (catching a waiter's or stranger's attention)
note: never say garçon; madame for a woman. Attaching monsieur/madame is what keeps it polite
the standard follow-up after ça va ?
huile d'olive; huile de tournesol for frying
j'ai soif = I'm thirsty
the polite decline when food appears
en = 'some of it' and can't be left out

note: The French hospitality reflex: coffee is offered the moment you sit down. tu veux boire quelque chose ? covers everything else.
de l' is the partitive – 'some'; you can't say just eau chaude
une petite cuillère = teaspoon
also the table napkin – context decides
je me douche also works; prendre un bain for a bath
réfrigérateur is the box-label word; everyone says frigo
opposite éteindre; also to light a candle
éteignez with vous

word: tu peux fermer / tu peux me passer …
roman: tu peux fermer / tu peux me passer …
note: French has no do-it-for-me verb pair like Hindi's dena – softening comes from tu peux …? and s'il te plaît

à + the body part, with contraction: au ventre, aux dents
point as you say it – works at any doctor's
mieux, never plus bien
at the chemist people say vous avez quelque chose contre la toux ?
tu viens d'où ? = where are you from?
chez + person: chez Marie, chez le médecin, chez nous. English has no single word for it
full form ne fais pas ça; ne faites pas ça with vous
en replaces the thing; written je n'en veux pas
ça m'a plu is the closer literal match and just as common
present tense does duty for the near future
or je peux trouver ça où ?

word: à la gare, s'il vous plaît
roman: à la gare, s'il vous plaît
note: you don't hail and negotiate – you get in and name the destination; the meter (le compteur) does the rest
what the shopkeeper says to you – learn it to recognise it
ce sera tout is the slightly more polished reply
éteindre covers the telly, the oven, the heating and the lights
entendre = hear, écouter = listen
answers: il fait beau, il pleut, il fait gris
cet après-midi = this afternoon; midi = midday
about you, not the weather – il fait froid is the weather
l'addition, s'il vous plaît. une facture is an invoice or utility bill

note: 70 = 60+10, 80 = 4×20, 97 = quatre-vingt-dix-sept. Belgium and Switzerland use septante and nonante instead – far easier, but not what you'll hear in France
huit heures et quart; quarter to is moins le quart – huit heures moins le quart
Nobody starts eating until it has been said, and you say it to strangers eating at the next table too. A waiter says it as your plate lands.
how family end calls and messages: allez, bisous ! gros bisous is warmer still
la carte is the list of dishes; le menu is a fixed-price set meal. Also la carte = the bank card and the map
Everyone says 'la CB' (say-bay): je paie en CB ?
j'ai envie d'un café / de sortir. This is what carries 'mann karna': desire lives in avoir, not in the verb
One word for every aunt, both sides of the family; French kinship ignores which parent she belongs to
'les cousins' covers the whole extended crowd at a family lunch
French has two levels where Hindi has three. The switch is negotiated out loud: tutoyer / vouvoyer. Let the older person offer
Bakery breakfast; 'croissant au beurre' is the proper one
Always plural; the standard quick home dinner
'jambon blanc' cooked, 'jambon cru' cured; the default sandwich filling
'steak-frites' is the café standard
A whole social institution: 'on prend l'apéro ?'. Short for l'apéritif
'une glace à la vanille'; the same word also means mirror
Masculine. Pronounced 'aye' (rhymes with paille): the -il is a yod, not a silent letter, so it is not simply 'l silent'. une gousse d'ail = a clove.
'sel et poivre'; 'poivré' = peppery
Free in every restaurant and you have to ask for it, otherwise you get billed bottled water
Shortened to 'un appart' in speech
'sortir la poubelle' = take the bin out
Its opposite is 'éteindre'; both work for lights, heating, TV and phones

word: avoir mal à + la partie du corps
roman: avoir mal à + la partie du corps
en: to have a pain in: j'ai mal à la tête / au dos / aux dents
note: à + le = au, à + les = aux. This one frame covers every ache you'll ever report
depuis takes the present tense: 'j'ai mal depuis deux jours'
aux fruits à coque = to nuts; aux arachides = to peanuts

word: il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?
roman: il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?
en: is there a pharmacy near here?
note: Spoken as 'y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?'
Also opens a new suggestion in conversation: 'sinon, on peut y aller demain'
The spoken default: 'y a plein de monde'. 'beaucoup de' is the neutral written one
Said as 'faut que j'y aille'. The standard way to leave a room or end a call
'c'est à dix minutes à pied' = it's ten minutes' walk
Also 'la place est prise ?' = is this seat taken
'j'arrive' means I'm nearly there, and is used very loosely
Also means a laptop; 'mon tél' in texts
Short for 'application'; feminine
'bon week-end !' on a Friday, to anyone at all
The first thing said in a French household in the morning, after bonjour. Answer: 'très bien, merci'

en: would you like something to drink?
note: The host's opening offer; 'je te sers quoi ?' once the bottles are out
Clipped from 'ne t'inquiète pas' and heard far more often than the full form; 'pas de souci' does the same job
'aller aux urgences'. This is the word you actually need in a crisis, more than hôpital

word: je me / tu te / il se / on se / vous vous
roman: je me / tu te / il se / on se / vous vous
en: reflexive verbs: je me lève, tu te reposes, on se voit demain
note: The pronoun changes with the subject and sits before the verb. It also carries 'each other': on se voit, on s'appelle. Every reflexive takes être in the past: je me suis levé.
The syllabus calls it ubiquitous in a note but never teaches it. du coup, on y va ? You will hear it every few sentences; donc is its tidier written cousin.
The commonest surprise noise in the language, and the thing you say to keep someone talking. ah d'accord = ah, I see.
Answers ça va ? without gushing, and also means a fair amount: il y a pas mal de monde.

en: linking a silent final consonant onto the next word: vous_avez, les_enfants, deux_ans
note: s and x link as 'z', d as 't' (quand il vient), f as 'v' (neuf heures). Never after et. This is why spoken French sounds like one long word rather than separate ones.
Any appointment, not a romantic one: j'ai rendez-vous chez le médecin à trois heures. No article after avoir: avoir rendez-vous. prendre rendez-vous = to book one.
The three courses, and how a set price is described: entrée + plat, or plat + dessert. Careful: an entrée is the starter, never the main. le plat du jour is the day's special.

word: une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît
roman: une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît
note: vous avez une table ? works too. In the evening ring ahead: j'ai réservé au nom de ...
un aller-retour pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît. un aller simple is a single, en seconde standard class. Buying a train ticket is core travel and the syllabus has no word for it.
j'ai quarante ans. Age is something you have, and the ans can never be dropped. Fine with children and close family; as nosy as in English with an adult.
silent z.

en: the one belonging to / the one that
note: celui de Marie = Marie's one; celle qui est là = the one that's over there. Agrees: celui, celle, ceux, celles.

en: the day after tomorrow / the day before yesterday
note: One word each in French where English needs five: après-demain, avant-hier. Both are perfectly ordinary in speech.
purely descriptive – there's no warm address term like bhabhi. You'd call her by her first name.
on the phone. ça coupe = you're breaking up; allô, tu m'entends ?
friendly and informal, roughly where yaar sits. mec is 'bloke' and lands younger; among family you'd just use first names.
French cooking leans on herbs – thym, laurier, persil – far more than on spices. les épices for spices proper.
Standard in France too, especially for family groups and calls abroad: le groupe famille. SMS and iMessage sit alongside it rather than replacing it. (As written this contradicted hs-0772.)
The volume pair: baisse le son / monte le son. For a person's voice it is parle moins fort. (Haggling belongs at hs-1044: shop and market prices in France are fixed.)
in speech plain de usually does it: on parle de toi

en: there's none left, we've run out
note: spoken: y en a plus; en stands in for the thing
on s'appelle en visio is what families say; FaceTime as a verb too
rent is a completely different word: le loyer
short for climatisation; many French homes simply don't have it

word: si tu veux, on y va
roman: si tu veux, on y va
note: si + present, never si + future: si tu viens demain, on mangera ensemble
French has no 'near me' possession construction – possession is just avoir; sur moi adds 'with me right now'
answer: c'est à moi, c'est à Paul
sur = on, touching (sur la table); de + le contracts to du: au-dessus du lit
the moment the relationship relaxes; answer oui, avec plaisir. vouvoyer = to use vous
ouais is the casual 'yeah'; French has no respect particle like ji
mutton (mouton) barely appears on French tables – agneau is the one you'll be offered
plain pain means a proper loaf – ask for pain de mie if you want the sliced stuff
The default brasserie order and the safe bet on any menu. Say how you want it: saignant, à point, bien cuit.
France's everyday snack – ham, butter, baguette, nothing else
des gâteaux secs on packets; un gâteau is a cake

en: set meal (starter + main, or main + dessert)
note: le menu in France means a fixed-price set meal, not the list of dishes
also the big breakfast bowl people drink coffee from
je t'envoie un mail ; tu me donnes ton adresse mail ? un courriel is the official word almost nobody says; un texto or un SMS for a text.
le placard = a built-in cupboard
a clock on the wall is une horloge or une pendule

en: can you put the heating on?
note: the French household equivalent of the Hindi 'put the fan on' – heating, not cooling
very spoken; complètement is the neutral one

en: how much is it to get to …?
note: you're asking, not haggling – French fares are metered or fixed
at a market stall, never handle the produce yourself – ask
answer oui, c'est sûr. bien sûr = of course is a different phrase

word: je suis allé(e) / je suis parti(e)
roman: je suis allé(e) / je suis parti(e)
en: être verbs in the past – and their agreement
note: movement and change verbs (aller, venir, partir, rester, naître, mourir) take être, and the participle agrees: elle est allée, on est arrivés

en: it'll be fine, it'll get done
note: very spoken reassurance; t'inquiète = don't worry
on va chez la belle-famille

word: je me souviens / je me souviens plus
roman: je me souviens / je me souviens plus
note: written je ne me souviens plus; je me rappelle is the same idea
the standard catch-up prompt on the phone
bon at the front signals you're wrapping up

école is primary; then le collège (11–15) and le lycée (15–18)
venir de + infinitive = the just-happened past. French has no separate present perfect – the passé composé covers both 'I ate' and 'I have eaten'

en: having done X; while doing X
note: après avoir + past participle for 'after doing'; en + -ant for two things at once: il parle en mangeant

the text you send when the traffic's bad
tata for an aunt; usually with a first name – tonton Marc

en: in-law and step relatives take beau- / belle-
note: the same forms cover in-laws and step-parents – context decides. No maternal/paternal split anywhere in the French system

en: all the best, hang in there
note: France has no elder's-blessing exchange; bon courage and bonne continuation are the warm things people send you off with
the other everyday version alongside joyeux anniversaire; clipped to bon anniv in texts
j'ai attrapé un rhume; enrhumé = bunged up
another avoir state, like j'ai faim
les urgences = A&E; 15 or 112 for an ambulance
il est fâché contre moi; vexé = miffed
the verb is aimer: je t'aime

en: good thing too, all the better
note: its opposite tant pis = never mind, is just as common

the standard way to end a phone call, usually followed by bisous

les informations in full; les nouvelles = news of a person

la monnaie is change; l'argent is money in general

the message you're expected to send after a journey

un comprimé on the box; la pilule is the contraceptive pill
how dosage gets explained at the chemist

word: quand je serai là, je t'appelle
roman: quand je serai là, je t'appelle

un distributeur (de billets); also a vending machine
from pull-over; un gilet is a cardigan

note: Market, bakery, cheese counter; 'c'est pour emporter' = it's a takeaway

Genuine dismay marker, not the tourist cliché; tone carries the meaning

word: c'est de la part de qui ?
